source.title: Stellar models: firm evidence, open questions and future developments

accepted.question_text: How can stellar evolution theory determine a physically grounded and empirically calibrated description of mass loss during the Red Giant Branch and Asymptotic Giant Branch stages for Population II giants, including the mass-loss timescales, the mechanisms that drive the mass loss, and how the efficiency depends on stellar parameters and metallicity, so that stellar model computations no longer rely on poorly justified extrapolations of prescriptions calibrated on Population I bright giants?
accepted.context_brief: Mass-loss law for RGB and AGB stars

evidence.quote: However, despite its importance, complete empirical determinations as well as a comprehensive physical description of the involved processes are still lacking.

From a theoretical point of view, our knowledge of the ML timescales, driving mechanisms, dependence on stellar parameters and metallicity is also very poor. The consequence is that there is little theoretical or observational guidance on how to incorporate ML into stellar model computations.

accepted.question_text: For red-giant-branch stars, is mass loss a continuous process or an episodic one, and how strongly, if at all, is the mass-loss behavior correlated with cluster metallicity?

evidence.quote: In addition, it seems that the ML phenomenon is not a continuous process along the RGB but an episodic phenomenon, and it does not appear to be strongly correlated with the cluster metallicity.

accepted.question_text: How can stellar evolutionary models provide a robust physical treatment of the third dredge-up in Thermally Pulsing Asymptotic Giant Branch stars by correctly describing convection and mixing across regions with strong composition and opacity discontinuities, so that the efficiency of the third dredge-up does not have to be represented by arbitrary methods and tunable free parameters?

evidence.quote: Concerning the 3DU, in spite of its fundamental relevance in determining the chemical enrichment of TPAGB star envelopes, its treatment in stellar evolutionary code is quite uncertain. This is due to the fact that we are not yet able to properly describe convection inside the stars, and in particular, in case of mixing occurring in a region with a strong composition/opacity discontinuity.

Many different - arbitrary - methods can be envisaged to treat the occurrence of the 3DU, but each one of these approaches has no robust physical ground. This has the important implication that in all fully evolutionary AGB models, the efficiency of the 3DU is managed by using one (or more) free parameter(s).

accepted.question_text: What quantitative changes do improved opacity tables for carbon-rich Asymptotic Giant Branch envelopes produce in the effective-temperature scale of AGB models, and how do those changes propagate into stellar-population-synthesis predictions that depend on AGB stars?
accepted.context_brief: C-rich opacity effects in AGB models

evidence.quote: These new opacities, although in good qualitative agreement with the previous estimates, show significant, quantitative differences. This occurrence has the effect that the Teff scale for AGB models is expected to be significantly affected, with consequences on SPS modeling that are still to be fully exploited.

accepted.question_text: What is the predictive power of synthetic Asymptotic Giant Branch models outside the parameter space covered by the populations used to calibrate them, given that these simulations still inherit the same unresolved physical problems as full evolutionary AGB models and require multiple parameters to be tuned by hand to match selected observations?
accepted.context_brief: Predictive power of synthetic AGB models

evidence.quote: As a consequence, in these synthetic simulations there is a number of free parameters that have to be tuned ‘by hand’ in order to reproduce some observational constraints such as for instance the Magellanic Clouds C-stars luminosity functions.

Synthetic AGB models constitute a much faster way to produce approximate models with these parameters tuned to match some observations, but it is not clear what their predictive power is, outside the parameter space covered by the calibrating AGB populations.

accepted.question_text: Is a solar-calibrated mixing-length parameter suitable for modeling Red Giant Branch stars across different metallicities, or do differences in input physics such as the equation of state and outer boundary conditions require a different calibration in order to reproduce empirical Red Giant Branch effective-temperature scales consistently?

evidence.quote: Therefore, it is important to verify that a solar αMLT is suitable also for RGB stars of various metallicities.

This comparison shows clearly that if one set of solar calibrated RGBs can reproduce a set of empirical RGB temperatures, the others cannot, and therefore in some case a solar calibrated αMLT value may not be adequate.

trace.notes: Mapped the PDF structure from the parsed full text. The paper has sections 1-4, with likely open-problem regions concentrated in section 4 ('Stellar models: the open problems') and a smaller unresolved-calibration issue in section 3.2 on RGB convection.
Extracted one implicit open question from the RGB discussion: whether a solar-calibrated mixing-length parameter remains valid across metallicities.

Extracted mass-loss candidates from section 4.1, including the general missing physical law and the specific unresolved issue of episodic versus continuous RGB mass loss and its metallicity dependence.
Extracted AGB-modeling candidates from section 4.2, covering third dredge-up physics, carbon-rich opacity consequences, and the extrapolative reliability of synthetic AGB models.
Expanded the paper's discussion of missing empirical and theoretical guidance on RGB/AGB mass loss into a standalone question covering calibration, mechanisms, and parameter dependence.
Kept the RGB continuity-versus-episodicity issue as a separate question because the source gives it as a distinct unresolved empirical claim.
Resolved the abbreviation 3DU as third dredge-up and inlined the role of convection, mixing, and free parameters to make the question self-contained.
Rewrote the source's statement about new carbon-rich opacity tables into a self-contained question about quantitative impact on AGB temperatures and SPS outputs.
Turned the source's warning about hand-tuned synthetic AGB models into a standalone question about out-of-sample predictive power.
Expanded the RGB αMLT calibration concern into a standalone question about portability of solar calibration across metallicities and input-physics choices.
Reviewed candidate overlap and kept six questions distinct: one RGB-convection calibration issue, two mass-loss questions, and three AGB-modeling questions. No near-duplicates required merging.
All accepted items are self-contained, use only source-supported claims, and include verbatim evidence with numeric PDF page citations. No item depended on unresolved cross-references.
